notation: Each tree is written as nested brackets [Function:Category#id{key=value|key=value} children]. The builder expands every tree into the hierarchical JSON embedded in the page. A child is a word of the displayed sentence, a nested node, or ~id for a gap linked to node id. Functions joined with + mark fusion. The root has no function.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N#kim{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP#vp [Predicator:V#laughed{form=preterite} laughed]]]
examples.explanation: Two separate questions get two separate answers. Kim is a noun (its category at word level), and that noun is the head of a one-word noun phrase. The NP Kim, not the noun on its own, is the subject of the clause. Likewise laughed is a verb functioning as predicator, and the one-word VP it heads is the predicate.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D#the The] [Head:Nom#nom [Mod:AdjP#adjp [Head:Adj old]] [Head:N#dog dog]]] [Predicate:VP#vp [Predicator:V barked] [Adjunct:AdvP#advp [Head:Adv loudly]]]]
examples.explanation: The subject is a whole phrase, the old dog, whose head is the noun dog. The determiner the and the modifier old depend on that head; they are not subjects themselves. Inside the predicate, loudly is an adverb phrase adding manner information: an adjunct that the verb bark does not require.

examples.text: Pat seems very fond of chocolate.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V seems] [PredComp:AdjP#adjp [Mod:AdvP [Head:Adv very]] [Head:Adj#fond fond] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep of] [Comp:NP [Head:N chocolate]]]]]]

predict.question: Which word is the head of very fond of chocolate?
predict.answer: fond. The phrase is an adjective phrase because its head is the adjective fond; very modifies it and of chocolate is its complement.

examples.explanation: Very fond of chocolate is one constituent, an adjective phrase headed by fond. Very is a modifier and of chocolate is a complement: fond in this sense needs an of-phrase (compare Pat seems fond of it with the odd Pat seems very fond, which is only possible when the context supplies what Pat is fond of). The whole AdjP is the predicative complement of seems.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#np [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj new]] [Head:N teacher]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V arrived] [Adjunct:AdvP#early [Head:Adv early]]]]
examples.explanation: The noun phrase the new teacher is the subject: it comes before the verb and is the phrase the verb agrees with (compare The new teachers arrive early). Early is an adverb here, an adjunct of time that could be left out.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V met] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj new]] [Head:N teacher]]]]]

predict.question: The phrase the new teacher is a noun phrase here too. What is its function?
predict.answer: Object. Same category as in The new teacher arrived early, different function: it follows the verb, it is required by met, and it could become the subject of a passive (The new teacher was met by Kim).

examples.explanation: The same noun phrase, the new teacher, now follows the verb and is its object. Its category has not changed; only its role in the containing clause has. The passive test confirms the object: The new teacher was met by Kim.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V became] [PredComp:NP#pc [Det:D a] [Head:N teacher]]]]

predict.question: Is a teacher an object here?
predict.answer: No. It is a predicative complement: it describes Kim rather than naming a second participant, and there is no passive (*A teacher was become by Kim).

examples.explanation: A teacher is a noun phrase, but it is not an object. It ascribes a property to the subject, Kim, so it is a predicative complement. It also has no passive counterpart, and it can be replaced by an adjective phrase (Kim became famous), which an object cannot.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V seems] [PredComp:AdjP#pc [Head:Adj#happy happy]]]]
examples.explanation: Happy is an adjective at word level and the head of a one-word adjective phrase. That AdjP is the predicative complement of seems. Compared with Kim became a teacher, the function is the same while the category differs: one predicative complement is an AdjP, the other an NP.

examples.text: Alex photographed the bird in the tree.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Alex]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V photographed] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:Nom [Head:N bird] [Mod:PP#pp [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N tree]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: On this reading the PP in the tree says which bird is meant, so it is a modifier inside the object NP: the bird in the tree is one constituent. The sentence is ambiguous, and the ambiguity lies entirely in constituent structure; the words are the same in both readings.

examples.text: Alex photographed the bird in the tree.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Alex]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V photographed] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:N bird]] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N tree]]]]]
examples.explanation: On this reading in the tree says where the photographing happened (perhaps Alex had climbed up). The PP is an adjunct in the VP, and the object is just the bird. The pronoun test separates the readings: Alex photographed it in the tree keeps only this one, because it replaces the whole object NP.

examples.text: Alex photographed it in the tree.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Alex]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V photographed] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N{form=pronoun} it]] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N tree]]]]]
examples.explanation: A pronoun stands for a whole NP. Because it cannot include in the tree, this sentence has only the adjunct reading. Substitution like this is evidence about which words form a constituent.

examples.text: The claim that Kim lied upset the committee.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#claim claim] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V lied]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V upset] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N committee]]]]
examples.explanation: Here that Kim lied gives the content of the claim, so the clause is a complement of the noun claim. Nothing is missing inside it: Kim lied is a complete clause, and that is a subordinator marking it as subordinate. The head noun licenses this complement; a noun such as table could not take one.

examples.text: The claim that Kim made was false.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#claim claim] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=integrated relative clause (that relative)} [Marker:Sbr that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V made] [Object:NP#gap ~claim]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj false]]]]
examples.explanation: This looks like the previous example but is a relative clause. Inside that Kim made the object of made is missing; it is understood as the claim. A relative clause modifies the head and can attach to almost any noun (the table that Kim made), whereas a content-clause complement needs a noun such as claim, fact or idea.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=3rd person singular present tense of the lexeme take} takes] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj early]] [Head:N bus]]]]]
examples.explanation: Takes is a word: one inflected form of the lexeme take, the dictionary item that also has the forms take, took, taking and taken. The -s ending marks present tense agreeing with a 3rd person singular subject. Grammatical rules refer to both levels: the lexeme determines that an object is possible, the form is chosen by tense and agreement.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=preterite of the lexeme take} took] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N bus]]]]
examples.explanation: Took is the preterite (past tense) form of take. It is a different word form from takes but the same lexeme, so a dictionary lists it under take. Irregular forms like took show that inflection is a matter of grammar, not just adding endings.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N#n{form=plural of the lexeme bus} buses]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=preterite plural of the lexeme be} were] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj late]]]]
examples.explanation: Buses is the plural form of the noun lexeme bus, and the verb form were agrees with that plural subject. Noun lexemes inflect for number (and for genitive case, as in bus's), while verb lexemes inflect for tense and related categories.

examples.tree: [Clause#main [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V thinks] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause (without that)} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left]]]]]
examples.explanation: The sentence contains two clauses: the whole thing, and Pat left, which is embedded as a complement of thinks. Pat left is a clause but not a sentence here; the sentence is the larger unit. The subordinator that is optional in this position (Kim thinks that Pat left).

examples.tree: [Coordination#co{cx=coordination of clauses} [Coord:Clause#c1 [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V stayed]]] [Coord:Clause#c2 [Marker:Crd#but but] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left]]]]]
examples.explanation: This sentence is a coordination of two clauses, so it has no single subject or predicate. Each coordinate is a clause; the coordinator but is a marker attached to the second coordinate. The comma is punctuation, not a constituent.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=canonical clause} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=preterite} bought] [Object:NP [Det:D a] [Head:N bike]]]]
examples.explanation: A canonical clause is the most elementary kind: a main clause, declarative, positive and with its parts in basic order. Describing such clauses first, and then each non-canonical variant (subordinate, interrogative, negative, passive and so on) by how it differs, is how the book organises its account of clauses.

examples.text: The bike was bought by Kim.
examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=passive clause (non-canonical)} [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N bike]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=preterite} was] [Comp:Clause{cx=past-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=past participle} bought] [Comp:PP#by{cx=internalised complement (by-phrase)} [Head:Prep by] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: This passive is non-canonical: it is described as a variant of the canonical Kim bought a bike. The object of the active corresponds to the passive subject, the bike, and Kim appears inside an optional PP with by. Be is followed by a past-participial clause.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun} They]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=plain present tense} take] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N train]]]]
examples.explanation: Take is the plain present tense form, used with subjects other than 3rd person singular. It sounds the same as the plain form in Take the train, but the two are distinguished by the constructions they occur in: this one is a tensed form that contrasts with took.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=imperative clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=plain form} Take] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N train]]]]
examples.explanation: This take is the plain form (no tense): the form of imperatives, subjunctives and infinitivals. The clause has no subject; the person addressed is understood as the one who would take the train. With be the two forms differ visibly: Be quiet, not Are quiet.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#aux{form=3rd person singular present tense; auxiliary} is] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=gerund-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=gerund-participle} taking] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N train]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Taking is the gerund-participle form. Here it follows progressive be, so traditional grammar would call it a present participle, but it is the same form that heads clauses like taking the train is cheaper. The auxiliary is carries the tense.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#aux{form=3rd person singular present tense; auxiliary} has] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=past-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=past participle} taken] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N train]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Has is an auxiliary verb in the perfect construction and taken is a past participle. The analysis followed here treats has as the predicator of the main VP, with taken the train as a non-finite clause complement. On this view, auxiliaries are verbs taking a complement, not mere markers attached to the lexical verb.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=3rd person singular present tense; lexical verb} has] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D a] [Head:N car]]]]
examples.explanation: Here have is a lexical verb of possession taking an object, not an auxiliary. In ordinary American and most British usage it takes do-support in questions and negatives (Does Kim have a car?; Kim doesn't have a car), which marks it as non-auxiliary in this use.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#aux{form=present tense; modal auxiliary} can] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=bare infinitival clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=plain form} swim]]]]]
examples.explanation: Can is a modal auxiliary. It has no plain form or participles (no *to can), it takes no -s agreement, and it is followed by a bare infinitival: swim is the plain form without to. The modal is the predicator; swim heads a non-finite clause complement.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=finite clause} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=preterite} left]]]
examples.explanation: A finite clause can stand alone as a sentence. Here finiteness shows in the tensed verb form left. In English, finiteness is treated as a property of the clause rather than simply of verb inflection, which matters for imperatives and subjunctives.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V wants] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=to-infinitival clause; catenative complement} [Predicate:VP#tovp [Marker:Sbr#to to] [Head:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=plain form} leave]]]]]]
examples.explanation: To leave is a non-finite clause: its verb is the plain form and it has no subject of its own (Kim is understood as the leaver). The word to is not a preposition here but the infinitival subordinator, a marker on the VP. The clause is a catenative complement of wants.

examples.text: It is essential that Kim be present.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#it [Head:N{form=pronoun; dummy it} It]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj essential]] [ExtSubj:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause, subjunctive} [Marker:Sbr that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#be{form=plain form} be] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj present]]]]]]]
examples.usage: The subjunctive be here is more usual in American English and in formal British English; British English often has Kim should be present instead.
examples.explanation: Be is the plain form, yet the clause that Kim be present is finite: it is a subjunctive clause with its own subject. This is why finiteness is defined for clauses, not verb forms. The content clause is extraposed; dummy it fills the subject position.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=declarative clause} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=preterite} closed] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:N door]]]]
examples.explanation: A declarative clause has a subject before the predicator and no special initial element. Declarative is the clause type; making a statement is the use it is characteristically put to, though not the only one.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=imperative clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} Close] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N door]]]]
examples.explanation: An imperative clause: plain-form verb and, here, no subject. Its characteristic use is a directive, but it can also be an invitation, advice or a wish, depending on context. The grammar classifies the form; the kind of speech act is a separate matter.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=exclamative clause} [Prenucleus:AdjP#p [Mod:AdvP [Head:Adv How]] [Head:Adj tall]] [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V has] [Comp:Clause{cx=past-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=past participle} grown] [PredComp:AdjP#gap ~p]]]]]]
examples.explanation: An exclamative clause begins with an exclamative phrase containing how or what. How tall is in prenucleus position; its role in the clause is predicative complement of grown, shown by the gap after grown. Notice there is no subject–auxiliary inversion, unlike the interrogative How tall has Kim grown?

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=declarative clause} [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N window]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj open]]]]
examples.context: Said by someone shivering, to a person standing next to the window.
examples.explanation: Grammatically this is a declarative clause. In the context given it may well be understood as a request to close the window: an indirect directive. Clause type is a matter of form; illocutionary force depends also on context.

examples.tree: [Clause#clause{cx=imperative clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} Sleep] [Adjunct:AdvP [Head:Adv well]]]]
examples.explanation: This is an imperative clause, but nobody is being ordered to do anything: it expresses a good wish. The imperative clause type is used for directives in the central case, not in all cases.

examples.text: Kim put the book on the shelf.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v put] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:N book]] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep on] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N shelf]]]]]

predict.question: Is on the shelf a complement or an adjunct?
predict.answer: A complement. Put requires a location phrase: Kim put the book is incomplete in ordinary use.

examples.explanation: The PP on the shelf is a complement: put requires it, and it is the verb put that licenses a goal location here. Omitting it leaves an incomplete clause (Kim put the book). Complements are licensed by particular heads; adjuncts are not.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V slept] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep on] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N train]]]]]

predict.question: Is on the train a complement or an adjunct?
predict.answer: An adjunct. Kim slept is complete, and a place phrase like this can go with almost any verb.

examples.explanation: On the train is a PP of the same shape as on the shelf in the previous example, but here it is an adjunct. Sleep does not require or select it; the clause is complete without it, and such a phrase could be added to almost any clause describing an event.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V lives] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Leeds]]]]]
examples.explanation: In the residence sense, live needs a locative phrase: Pat lives is odd unless it means 'is alive'. So in Leeds is a complement here, even though location phrases are more often adjuncts.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V met] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Leeds]]]]]
examples.explanation: With met, in Leeds is optional and simply locates the event: an adjunct. Compare Pat lives in Leeds, where the identical PP is a complement. The function comes from the relation to the verb, not from the phrase itself.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v relied] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep#on on] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]]]]]
examples.explanation: Rely selects a PP headed specifically by on: a prepositional verb. On Kim is a complement because the verb chooses the preposition; no other preposition will do (*relied at Kim). Kim is the complement of on, not an object of relied.

examples.text: The box under the stairs is heavy.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#box box] [Mod:PP [Head:Prep under] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N{form=plural} stairs]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=3rd person singular present tense} is] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj heavy]]]]
examples.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject, and the subject is the whole NP the box under the stairs. Agreement is with that NP's head, box, which is singular, so the verb is is, even though the plural noun stairs stands right next to it.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V broke] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:N window]]]]
examples.explanation: Kim is the subject and also the agent, the one who performs the action. In a canonical active clause like this, the agent is chosen as subject. Subject is a syntactic function; agent is a semantic role. They often coincide but are different kinds of notion.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N window]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V broke]]]
examples.explanation: The window is the subject, but it is not an agent: it undergoes the breaking. Subject status here rests on syntax (position before the verb, agreement in The windows break), not on who acts.

examples.text: The window was broken by Kim.
examples.tree: [Clause{cx=passive clause} [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N window]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=preterite} was] [Comp:Clause{cx=past-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=past participle} broken] [Comp:PP#by{cx=internalised complement (by-phrase)} [Head:Prep by] [Comp:NP#agent [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Kim is still the agent but is no longer the subject: it is the complement of the preposition by. The subject of the passive is the window. Changing voice changes which participant is subject without changing semantic roles.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D This] [Head:N key]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V opened] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N door]]]]
examples.explanation: The subject this key denotes an instrument, not an agent. Subjects of active clauses can have a range of semantic roles; what they share is syntactic behaviour.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V gave] [Oi:NP#oi [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Od:NP#od [Det:D a] [Head:N book]]]]

predict.question: Which NP is the indirect object?
predict.answer: Pat. In a ditransitive clause the indirect object comes first and typically denotes the recipient.

examples.explanation: A ditransitive clause has two objects. Pat, the recipient, is the indirect object and comes first; a book is the direct object. Both are NPs directly in the VP, with no preposition.

examples.text: Kim gave a book to Pat.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V gave] [Object:NP#od [Det:D a] [Head:N book]] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep to] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]]]]]
examples.explanation: Pat is again the recipient, but syntactically to Pat is a PP complement, not an indirect object. Indirect objects are NPs. The meaning is close to Kim gave Pat a book, yet the structure differs: this clause is monotransitive with one object plus a PP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N news]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V made] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [PredComp:AdjP#pc [Head:Adj angry]]]]
examples.explanation: This is a complex-transitive clause: an object, Pat, and a predicative complement, angry, which describes the object rather than the subject. The PC is related to the object just as angry relates to the subject in Pat is angry.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N club]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V elected] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [PredComp:NP#pc [Head:N treasurer]]]]
examples.explanation: Two NPs follow the verb, but only Kim is an object. Treasurer is a predicative complement giving the role Kim comes to hold. Unlike a ditransitive's second object it cannot become a passive subject (*Treasurer was elected Kim), and it can lack a determiner because it denotes a role.

examples.tree: [Clause{cx=ascriptive copular clause} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:NP#pc [Det:D a] [Head:N doctor]]]]
examples.explanation: In this ascriptive use of be, a doctor ascribes a property to Kim: being a doctor. You cannot swap the two NPs without changing the kind of statement (A doctor is Kim is very odd).

examples.tree: [Clause{cx=specifying copular clause} [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N winner]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:NP#pc [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]]]]
examples.explanation: This is the specifying use of be: the subject sets up a variable (who won?) and the predicative complement, Kim, supplies its value. Specifying clauses are typically reversible, Kim was the winner, with the NPs switching functions.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V looked] [Comp:PP#up [Head:Prep up]] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:N word]]]]
examples.explanation: Up is a particle: an intransitive preposition functioning as complement, forming an idiom with look. The word is the object of looked, not the complement of up. The particle can follow the object (Kim looked the word up), and must do so when the object is a pronoun (Kim looked it up).

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V looked] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep up] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N chimney]]]]]
examples.explanation: Here up the chimney is a single PP: up takes the chimney as its complement and the phrase gives the direction of looking. It can be fronted as a unit (Up the chimney Kim looked) and up cannot move after the NP (*Kim looked the chimney up, in this sense).

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V put] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D the] [Head:N cat]] [Comp:PP#out [Head:Prep out]]]]
examples.explanation: Out is an intransitive preposition functioning as complement of put, here after the object. Kim put out the cat has the same constituents in a different order; the particle position varies, which is characteristic of the verb–particle–object construction.

examples.text: The tall woman in the corner is my aunt.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D#the The] [Head:Nom#nom [Mod:AdjP#pre [Head:Adj tall]] [Head:N#woman woman] [Mod:PP#post [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N corner]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:NP#pc [Det:NP#my{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} my]] [Head:N aunt]]]]
examples.explanation: The subject NP has a determiner, a head noun woman, and modifiers on both sides: tall before the head and in the corner after it. The modifiers combine with the head to form a nominal (tall woman in the corner), and the determiner the combines with that nominal to form the NP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D#three{form=cardinal numeral} Three] [Head:N students]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V passed]]]
examples.explanation: Three is a determinative, the category that also includes the, a, some and every. Here it functions as determiner of the NP, marking it as indefinite and giving the number.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D#the The] [Head:Nom [Mod:DP#mod [Head:D#three{form=cardinal numeral} three]] [Head:N students]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V passed]]]
examples.explanation: Three is still a determinative, but the determiner function is now filled by the, so three is a modifier within the nominal. Category stays fixed; function depends on the position in the containing structure.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V has] [Object:NP#obj [Det:D#enough enough] [Head:N money]]]]
examples.explanation: Enough is a determinative functioning as determiner of the NP enough money. Determinative names a category of words; determiner names a function in the NP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N room]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP#adjp [Head:Adj big] [Mod:DP#mod [Head:D#enough enough]]]]]
examples.explanation: The same determinative, enough, here follows an adjective and modifies it. It is not a determiner, because there is no NP for it to determine. This is why the category (determinative) and the function (determiner) need separate names.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V feels] [PredComp:AdjP#adjp [Mod:DP#mod [Head:D#much much]] [Head:Adj{form=comparative} better]]]]
examples.explanation: Much is a degree determinative. Before a comparative adjective it functions as a modifier, not as a determiner. Compare much water, where much is determiner of an NP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:NP#gen{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=proper noun, genitive} Kim's]] [Head:N bike]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=preterite} was] [Comp:Clause{cx=past-participial clause (passive)} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=past participle} stolen]]]]]
examples.explanation: The determiner function is filled not by a determinative but by a genitive NP, Kim's. Like the, it makes the NP definite (Kim's bike means a particular bike), and the two cannot combine (*the Kim's bike). Because it also has a subject-like relation to the head (Kim is the possessor of the bike), it is called a subject-determiner.

examples.text: Some guests left early, but most stayed.
examples.tree: [Coordination{cx=coordination of clauses} [Coord:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D Some] [Head:N guests]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left] [Adjunct:AdvP [Head:Adv early]]]] [Coord:Clause [Marker:Crd but] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP#most [Det+Head:D#mostw most]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V stayed]]]]]
examples.explanation: Most is a whole NP, the subject of stayed, understood as most guests. There is no separate head noun: the determinative most combines the determiner function with the head function. This is a fused determiner-head.

examples.text: Kim chose the red shirt, and Pat chose the blue.
examples.tree: [Coordination{cx=coordination of clauses} [Coord:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V chose] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj red]] [Head:N shirt]]]]] [Coord:Clause [Marker:Crd and] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V chose] [Object:NP#np [Det:D the] [Mod+Head:Adj#blue blue]]]]]]
examples.explanation: The blue means the blue shirt. The adjective blue does double duty as modifier and head: a fused modifier-head. It remains an adjective rather than becoming a noun: even with plural shirts it would stay the blue, not the blues.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N#she{form=pronoun, nominative} She]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V thanked] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N#him{form=pronoun, accusative} him]]]]
examples.explanation: Pronouns are treated as a subclass of nouns: she and him head NPs just as Kim does, with the case form showing function (nominative she as subject, accusative him as object). Unlike most nouns, pronouns rarely take determiners or modifiers.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V blamed] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N#refl{form=reflexive pronoun} herself]]]]
examples.explanation: Herself is a reflexive pronoun heading the object NP. Its interpretation is tied to the subject in the same clause: Pat blamed Pat. A plain pronoun (Pat blamed her) would normally refer to someone else.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D A] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP#attr [Head:Adj happy]] [Head:N child]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=preterite; auxiliary} was] [Comp:Clause{cx=gerund-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=gerund-participle} singing]]]]]
examples.explanation: Happy is used attributively: an AdjP functioning as pre-head modifier inside a nominal. Attributive modification is one of the two central functions of adjectives.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N child]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP#pred [Head:Adj happy]]]]
examples.explanation: The same adjective is now used predicatively, as predicative complement of be. Most adjectives can be used both attributively and predicatively, which is one test for the category.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP#attr [Head:Adj main]] [Head:N reason]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:NP [Head:N money]]]]
examples.explanation: Main is an attributive-only adjective: it occurs as modifier before a noun but not predicatively (*The reason was main). It is still an adjective; it just has a restricted range of functions.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N child]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP#pred [Head:Adj afraid]]]]
examples.explanation: Afraid works the other way round: it is a never-attributive adjective, fine as predicative complement but not before a noun (*an afraid child; a frightened child is used instead). It can take modifiers such as very and complements like of the dark, as adjectives do.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N members] [Mod:AdjP#post [Head:Adj present]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V voted]]]
examples.usage: Formal, especially in reports of meetings.
examples.explanation: Present here follows the noun it modifies: a postpositive adjective. In the sense 'in attendance' it is restricted to this position and to predicative use (The members were present); the present members would be understood differently.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V sounded] [PredComp:AdjP#pc [Head:Adj calm]]]]
examples.explanation: Calm is an adjective phrase functioning as predicative complement of sound: it describes Kim. Sound is a complex-intransitive verb like seem, which takes an AdjP, not an adverb (*Kim sounded calmly, in this sense).

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V spoke] [Adjunct:AdvP#adj [Head:Adv calmly]]]]
examples.explanation: Calmly is an adverb: it describes the manner of speaking and functions as an adjunct. Adverbs typically modify verbs (and the VPs they head), adjectives and other adverbs, but not nouns.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V drives] [Adjunct:AdvP#adj [Head:Adv#fast fast]]]]
examples.explanation: Fast has no -ly, yet here it is an adverb modifying the verb, as manner adjunct. The same spelling is an adjective in a fast car. The -ly ending is typical of adverbs but neither necessary nor sufficient (compare the adjective friendly).

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V answered] [Adjunct:AdvP#advp [Mod:AdvP [Head:Adv surprisingly]] [Head:Adv#quickly quickly]]]]
examples.explanation: Surprisingly quickly is an adverb phrase headed by quickly, with surprisingly as its modifier. AdvPs are structurally simple: mostly a head with an optional modifier, and complements only with a few adverbs.

examples.text: Pat gave a remarkably calm reply.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V gave] [Object:NP [Det:D a] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP#adjp [Mod:AdvP#advp [Head:Adv remarkably]] [Head:Adj calm]] [Head:N reply]]]]]
examples.explanation: Remarkably modifies the adjective calm, not the noun reply: the AdjP remarkably calm is the modifier of reply. An adverb can sit inside an NP this way only as a dependent of an adjective.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep#before before] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N meeting]]]]]
examples.explanation: Before is a preposition taking an NP complement, the meeting. The PP is a time adjunct. So far this matches the traditional picture of prepositions.

examples.text: Kim left before the meeting ended.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep#before before] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N meeting]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V ended]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Traditional grammar calls this before a subordinating conjunction. The analysis here keeps it a preposition: the same word with the same meaning, now taking a clause as its complement. Verbs take NP or clause complements without changing category; prepositions are treated the same way.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N{form=plural} children]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V played] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep#outside outside]]]]
examples.explanation: Outside has no complement here, but it is still a preposition: an intransitive one, just as some verbs occur without objects. Traditional grammar would call it an adverb. Compare played outside the house, where the same word takes an NP complement.

examples.text: The children played outside the house.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N{form=plural} children]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V played] [Adjunct:PP#pp [Head:Prep#outside outside] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N house]]]]]
examples.explanation: Outside the house is a PP: preposition plus NP complement. Since outside means the same with or without the NP, it makes sense to give it the same category in both uses.

examples.text: Kim left because the room was cold.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left] [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=reason adjunct} [Head:Prep#because because] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N room]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj cold]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Because is a preposition heading a PP of reason; its complement is a content clause. Unlike the subordinator that, because contributes meaning of its own and heads the phrase.

examples.text: Kim said that the room was cold.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V said] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr#that that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N room]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj cold]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: That is a subordinator, a marker of the subordinate clause rather than its head. It adds no meaning and is often omissible (Kim said the room was cold). Because, by contrast, carries meaning, cannot be omitted and heads its PP.

examples.text: Kim cut the bread with a sharp knife.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V cut] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N bread]] [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=instrument adjunct} [Head:Prep with] [Comp:NP [Det:D a] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj sharp]] [Head:N knife]]]]]]
examples.explanation: With a sharp knife names the instrument used. It is an adjunct: optional, and possible with any verb denoting a suitable action.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Adjunct:AdvP#freq{cx=frequency adjunct} [Head:Adv usually]] [Predicator:V travels] [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=means adjunct} [Head:Prep by] [Comp:NP [Head:N bus]]]]]
examples.explanation: By bus gives the means of travel and usually gives frequency; both are adjuncts. Usually sits before the verb but still inside the predicate, so the VP here has an adjunct on each side of its predicator.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Adjunct:AdvP#adv{cx=manner adjunct} [Head:Adv carefully]] [Predicator:V wrapped] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N vase]]]]
examples.explanation: Carefully describes the manner of wrapping. Manner adjuncts can precede or follow the VP they modify (Pat wrapped the vase carefully), without changing their function.

examples.tree: [Clause [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=temporal location adjunct} [Head:Prep On] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Monday]]] [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V visited] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]]]]
examples.explanation: On Monday locates the event in time and is an adjunct. Placed at the front, it is a dependent of the clause rather than of the VP; the comma is punctuation. Compare the same PP at the end of the VP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V visited] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=temporal location adjunct} [Head:Prep on] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Monday]]]]]
examples.explanation: The same time adjunct at the end of the VP. Its function is unchanged; only its position and attachment differ, which can affect emphasis and how it is understood with other material.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N meeting]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:PP#pp [Head:Prep on] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Monday]]]]]
examples.explanation: After be, on Monday is not an adjunct: The meeting is would be incomplete. The temporal PP is the predicative complement of be. A phrase with the meaning of time location can thus be either complement or adjunct, depending on the construction.

examples.text: The game stopped because of the rain.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N game]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V stopped] [Adjunct:PP#pp{cx=reason adjunct} [Head:Prep because] [Comp:PP [Head:Prep of] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N rain]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Because here takes a PP complement headed by of. With a clause complement it would be because it rained. Either way because is the head of a PP functioning as a reason adjunct.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V knows] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr#that that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V left]]]]]]
examples.explanation: That Pat left is a declarative content clause, a complement of know. It consists of the marker that plus a head clause. The analysis followed here reserves the term object for NPs, so the content clause is simply a complement of the verb.

examples.text: That the shop closed surprised Kim.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr#that That] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N shop]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V closed]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V surprised] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]]]]
examples.usage: Rather formal; the extraposed version is far more common in speech.
examples.explanation: Here the content clause is the subject. In subject position that cannot be omitted (*The shop closed surprised Kim), unlike after a verb such as know.

examples.text: It surprised Kim that the shop closed.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#it [Head:N{form=pronoun; dummy it} It]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V surprised] [Object:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [ExtSubj:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N shop]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V closed]]]]]]
examples.explanation: The content clause has been extraposed: it appears at the end as an extraposed subject, and the subject position is filled by a dummy it that refers to nothing. Extraposition moves heavy material to the end, where new information tends to go.

examples.text: It is obvious that Kim lied.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#it [Head:N{form=pronoun; dummy it} It]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj obvious]] [ExtSubj:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V lied]]]]]]

predict.question: What does it refer to in this sentence?
predict.answer: Nothing. It is a dummy subject; the content of what is obvious is given by the extraposed clause that Kim lied.

examples.explanation: It is a dummy pronoun, the syntactic subject. The clause that Kim lied is the extraposed subject; the non-extraposed version is That Kim lied is obvious.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:Clause#cc{cx=declarative content clause} [Marker:Sbr That] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V lied]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj obvious]]]]
examples.explanation: The basic version: the content clause is itself the subject. It and the extraposed variant mean the same; they package the information differently.

examples.text: Kim asked whether the shop was open.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V asked] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=closed interrogative content clause} [Marker:Sbr#whether whether] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N shop]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj open]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: This is a subordinate closed interrogative: it corresponds to the yes/no question Was the shop open? Whether is a subordinator marking it. Subordinate interrogatives have no subject–auxiliary inversion in standard English.

examples.text: Pat wondered if the shop was open.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V wondered] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=closed interrogative content clause} [Marker:Sbr#if if] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N shop]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj open]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Interrogative if is a subordinator like whether, and here the two are interchangeable. If is more restricted: it is not used at the start of a subject clause (Whether it rains is unclear, not *If it rains is unclear). This if is a different item from the conditional preposition if.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V asked] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=open interrogative content clause} [Prenucleus:NP#who [Head:N{form=interrogative pronoun} who]] [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V invited] [Object:NP#gap ~who]]]]]]
examples.usage: Whom instead of who is possible here in formal style.
examples.explanation: A subordinate open interrogative: it corresponds to the question Who did Pat invite? Who is in prenucleus position and is understood as the object of invited, marked by the gap. Asking is about a variable: the answer would name the person.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V ate] [Object:NP#np{cx=fused relative construction} [Head+Prenucleus:D#what{form=relative determinative} what] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=relative clause (fused)} [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V cooked] [Object:NP#gap ~what]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: What Pat cooked is an NP, not a clause: it denotes the food, and Kim ate it. What is fused: it is at once the head of the NP and the prenucleus of the relative clause, roughly 'the thing that Pat cooked'. It is the object of ate, and inside the relative clause it is understood as the object of cooked.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V asked] [Comp:Clause#cc{cx=open interrogative content clause} [Prenucleus:NP#whatnp [Det+Head:D#what{form=interrogative determinative} what]] [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V cooked] [Object:NP#gap ~whatnp]]]]]]
examples.explanation: With asked, what Pat cooked is an interrogative clause: Kim asked a question, not about food in general but which thing Pat cooked. The string is identical to the fused relative in Kim ate what Pat cooked, but the category differs: here a clause, there an NP. Kim ate something; Kim asked a question.

examples.text: The cake which Kim baked was delicious.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#cake cake] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=integrated relative clause (wh relative)} [Prenucleus:NP#wh [Det+Head:D#which{form=relative determinative} which]] [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V baked] [Object:NP#gap ~wh]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj delicious]]]]
examples.explanation: A wh relative: the relative word which stands in prenucleus position and is linked to the gap after baked. The relative clause modifies cake within the nominal, telling us which cake is meant.

examples.text: The cake that Kim baked was delicious.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#cake cake] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=integrated relative clause (that relative)} [Marker:Sbr#that that] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V baked] [Object:NP#gap ~cake]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj delicious]]]]
examples.explanation: Here that is analysed as a subordinator, the same word as in content clauses, not as a relative pronoun. One reason: unlike which, it cannot follow a preposition (*the shelf on that Kim put it). The relativised element is simply the gap after baked, understood via the head noun.

examples.text: The cake Kim baked was delicious.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#cake cake] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=integrated relative clause (bare relative)} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V baked] [Object:NP#gap ~cake]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj delicious]]]]
examples.explanation: A bare relative has neither a relative word nor that. The clause Kim baked still modifies cake and still contains a gap. Bare relatives are possible when the gap is not the subject of the relative clause.

examples.text: The person Kim talked to was Pat.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N#person person] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=integrated relative clause (bare relative)} [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V talked] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep#to to] [Comp:NP#gap ~person]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]]]]
examples.explanation: The preposition to is stranded: its complement is a gap, understood as the person. Preposition stranding is fully standard in English; the alternative the person to whom Kim talked is more formal.

examples.text: The student who won the prize thanked her teachers.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:Nom [Head:N student] [Mod:Clause#rel{cx=integrated relative clause (wh relative)} [Prenucleus:NP#who [Head:N{form=relative pronoun} who]] [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP#gap ~who] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V won] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N prize]]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V thanked] [Object:NP [Det:NP{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} her]] [Head:N{form=plural} teachers]]]]
examples.explanation: An integrated relative clause: it identifies which student is meant, is spoken without separate intonation, and is not set off by commas. Without it, the student would not be identified.

examples.text: My sister, who lives in Leeds, phoned.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:NP{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} My]] [Head:N#sister sister]] [Supplement:Clause#rel{cx=supplementary relative clause|anchor=subj} [Prenucleus:NP#who [Head:N{form=relative pronoun} who]] [Nucleus:Clause [Subject:NP#gap ~who] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V lives] [Comp:PP [Head:Prep in] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Leeds]]]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V phoned]]]
examples.explanation: A supplementary relative clause adds information about a referent already identified (my sister); it is set off by commas or separate intonation. It is a supplement anchored to the NP my sister, not a modifier inside it, so the subject is just my sister.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V enjoys] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=gerund-participial clause; catenative complement} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=gerund-participle} swimming]]]]]
examples.explanation: Swimming is a verb, the gerund-participle form, heading a non-finite clause that is the catenative complement of enjoys. It is a verb because it can take an object and adverb modifiers (enjoys swimming lengths slowly), not determiners or adjectives.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:Clause#nf{cx=gerund-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=gerund-participle} Swimming]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:NP [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj good]] [Head:N exercise]]]]]
examples.explanation: The subject is a gerund-participial clause consisting of just a predicate. Its head is still a verb: compare Swimming long distances is good exercise, where swimming takes an object, something nouns cannot do.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N#n{form=noun ending in -ing} singing]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V was] [PredComp:AdjP [Head:Adj beautiful]]]]
examples.explanation: Here singing is a noun, not a verb: it takes the determiner the and would take adjectives (the beautiful singing) and an of-phrase (the singing of the choir), but not an object or adverb. Nouns in -ing are a distinct category from gerund-participles.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:Clause#nf{cx=gerund-participial clause} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=gerund-participle} Singing] [Adjunct:AdvP [Head:Adv loudly]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V annoys] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N{form=plural} neighbours]]]]
examples.explanation: Singing is a verb here: it is modified by the adverb loudly, as verbs are, and the whole subject is a clause. Compare the noun in The loud singing annoys the neighbours, which takes a determiner and an adjective instead.

examples.text: Kim longed for the rain to stop.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V longed] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=to-infinitival clause with subject} [Marker:Sbr#for for] [Head:Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N rain]] [Predicate:VP [Marker:Sbr to] [Head:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} stop]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: For the rain to stop is a single to-infinitival clause with its own subject, the rain. For is a clause subordinator, not a preposition taking the rain as its complement: the rain is the subject of to stop, and what Kim longed for is the whole event of the rain stopping.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N joke]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V made] [Object:NP#obj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=bare infinitival clause; catenative complement} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} laugh]]]]]
examples.explanation: Laugh is a bare infinitival (plain form, no to) after make in the active. Kim is the object of made and is understood as the subject of laugh: a complex catenative construction, with an intervening NP.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:AdjP#adjp [Head:Adj keen] [Comp:Clause#nf{cx=to-infinitival clause} [Predicate:VP [Marker:Sbr to] [Head:VP [Predicator:V{form=plain form} help]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: Here a to-infinitival is the complement of an adjective, keen, inside the AdjP. Non-finite clauses occur as complements of verbs, adjectives and nouns alike.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:Coordination#co{cx=coordination of NPs} [Coord:NP#c1 [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Coord:NP#c2 [Marker:Crd#and and] [Head:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]]]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V arrived]]]
examples.explanation: The subject is a coordination of two NPs. Each coordinate has the same function relative to the verb; neither is the head of the other. The coordinator and is a marker belonging to the second coordinate, which is why Kim and is not a constituent while and Pat is.

examples.text: Kim is a lawyer and very proud of it.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V is] [PredComp:Coordination#co{cx=coordination of unlike categories (NP and AdjP)} [Coord:NP#c1 [Det:D a] [Head:N lawyer]] [Coord:AdjP#c2 [Marker:Crd and] [Head:AdjP [Mod:AdvP [Head:Adv very]] [Head:Adj proud] [Comp:PP [Head:Prep of] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun} it]]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: The two coordinates belong to different categories, an NP and an AdjP. They can still be coordinated because each could serve on its own as predicative complement of be. Coordination depends on shared function, not identical category.

examples.text: Kim, my neighbour, fixed the fence.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Supplement:NP#sup{cx=appositive supplement|anchor=subj} [Det:NP{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} my]] [Head:N neighbour]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V fixed] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N fence]]]]
examples.explanation: My neighbour is a supplement: an NP loosely attached to its anchor Kim and set off by commas. It is not a coordinate (the verb would still be singular with a present-tense verb: Kim, my neighbour, fixes fences), and it is not part of the subject NP. Leaving it out leaves a complete sentence with the same structure.

examples.text: Kim fixed the fence – a difficult job.
examples.tree: [Clause#anchor [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V fixed] [Object:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N fence]]] [Supplement:NP#sup{cx=supplement anchored to a clause|anchor=anchor} [Det:D a] [Head:Nom [Mod:AdjP [Head:Adj difficult]] [Head:N job]]]]
examples.explanation: Here the supplement a difficult job comments on the whole event, so its anchor is the clause Kim fixed the fence rather than any NP in it. Supplements are not dependents: they are attached more loosely than modifiers or complements, and are usually marked off by dashes, commas or brackets.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V received] [Object:NP [Det:D a] [Head:N letter]]]]
examples.explanation: Pat is subject, but semantically a recipient rather than an agent: Pat did nothing to bring the letter. With receive the recipient is subject, while with send it is the sender.

examples.text: The letter was sent on Monday.
examples.tree: [Clause{cx=passive clause} [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N letter]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=preterite} was] [Comp:Clause{cx=past-participial clause (short passive)} [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V{form=past participle} sent] [Adjunct:PP#time{cx=temporal location adjunct} [Head:Prep on] [Comp:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Monday]]]]]]]
examples.explanation: A short passive: there is no by-phrase, so the agent is left unexpressed. Passives are often used exactly for this, when the agent is unknown or unimportant. The letter is the subject although it corresponds to the object of the active (Someone sent the letter).

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Det:D The] [Head:N rain]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v stopped]]]
examples.explanation: Stopped is a verb functioning as predicator. Words like rain, which can be nouns or verbs, show why category is decided by behaviour: here rain takes a determiner, the, and heads the subject NP, so it is a noun.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#it [Head:N{form=pronoun; dummy it} It]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V#v{form=preterite} rained] [Adjunct:NP#dur{cx=duration adjunct} [Det:D all] [Head:N night]]]]
examples.explanation: Rained is a verb: it carries tense and heads the predicate. Its subject it is a dummy that refers to nothing. All night is an NP functioning as an adjunct of duration: NPs as well as PPs and AdvPs can be adjuncts.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Head:N{form=proper noun} Sam]] [Predicate:VP#vp [Predicator:V#v{form=3rd person singular present tense} sings] [Adjunct:AdvP#adj [Head:Adv beautifully]]]]
examples.explanation: The predicate sings beautifully is a VP headed by the verb sings. The predicate is the head of the clause, and the predicator is the head of the VP. Beautifully is a dependent inside the VP.

examples.text: They bought a very old house.
examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=pronoun} They]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V bought] [Object:NP#np [Det:D a] [Head:Nom#nom [Mod:AdjP#adjp [Mod:AdvP [Head:Adv very]] [Head:Adj#old old]] [Head:N#house house]]]]]
examples.explanation: Very old is one constituent: very modifies old, not house (there is no *a very house). The AdjP very old then modifies house. Heads choose their dependents, and the dependents of a dependent stay inside its phrase.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP#subj [Det:D The] [Head:N{form=plural} children]] [Predicate:VP#vp [Predicator:V#v opened] [Object:NP#obj [Det:NP{form=genitive; subject-determiner} [Head:N{form=pronoun, genitive} their]] [Head:N{form=plural} presents]]]]
examples.explanation: The clause divides into subject (the children) and predicate (opened their presents). Within the predicate, opened is the predicator and their presents its object. Their is a genitive pronoun in determiner function.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Pat]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V looked] [Comp:PP#pp [Head:Prep at] [Comp:NP [Det:D the] [Head:N map]]]]]
examples.explanation: Look in this sense selects a PP headed by at: a prepositional verb. The map is the complement of at, so at the map is a PP complement, not an object of looked. Yet the passive The map was looked at is possible, with the preposition stranded.

examples.tree: [Clause [Subject:NP [Head:N{form=proper noun} Kim]] [Predicate:VP [Predicator:V arrived] [Adjunct:AdvP#time{cx=temporal location adjunct} [Head:Adv recently]]]]
examples.explanation: Recently locates the arrival in time. It is an adjunct; the clause is complete without it. Its category is a separate question from its function: time adjuncts may be AdvPs like this one, PPs (on Monday) or NPs (last week).

contrasts.explanation: Both are the NP the new teacher, so the category is identical. In the first it is the subject (before the verb, the verb agrees with it); in the second it is the object of met. Function is a relation to the containing clause, not a property of the phrase.

Both follow the verb and both are NPs. The object of met denotes a second participant and can be the subject of a passive. The predicative complement of became describes Kim, has no passive, and alternates with an AdjP (Kim became famous).
Same function, different category: each is a predicative complement, but one is an NP and the other an AdjP. A label like 'predicative adjective' merges two independent questions.
Both are locative PPs at the end of the VP. On the shelf is required by put and so is a complement; on the train is optional with slept and could combine with almost any verb, so it is an adjunct.
The identical PP in Leeds is a complement of lives (Pat lives is incomplete in this sense) but an adjunct with met. Whether a dependent is a complement depends on the head it combines with.
On Monday is predicative complement of be in the first (the clause needs it) and an optional time adjunct in the second.
Pat is the recipient in both, but only in the first is it an indirect object. In the second the recipient is expressed by the PP to Pat, a complement of a different category and function.
Enough is a determinative in both. In enough money it is the determiner of an NP; in big enough it is a post-head modifier in an AdjP. Determinative is the category, determiner the function.
Three is a determinative in both. Alone it is the determiner; after the, which takes the determiner function, it becomes a modifier within the nominal.

Calm is an adjective phrase describing Kim, as predicative complement of sounded. Calmly is an adverb phrase describing the manner of speaking, as an adjunct. The choice follows from function: sound takes a predicative complement, speak takes a manner adjunct.

Singing is a verb in the first (modified by an adverb, heading a clause) and a noun in the second (with a determiner, heading an NP). The tests are about dependents: adverbs and objects go with verbs, determiners and adjectives with nouns.

The same words, what Pat cooked, are an NP in the first (the thing Pat cooked, which Kim ate) and an interrogative clause in the second (the question which thing Pat cooked). Paraphrases show the difference: the thing that Pat cooked fits only the first; which thing Pat cooked only the second.
Both follow claim and begin with that. The relative clause has a gap (made what? the claim) and modifies the noun; the content clause is complete and expresses the claim's content as a complement.
That is a meaningless, often omissible marker of a content clause. Because carries meaning, cannot be omitted and heads a PP whose complement is the clause.

Kim is the agent in both sentences, but only in the active is it the subject. In the passive the subject is the window and Kim is the complement of by. Subject is a syntactic function; agent is a semantic role.

In the coordination both Kim and Pat are coordinates of the subject, which counts as plural. In the supplement, my neighbour adds information about Kim but is not part of the subject; the subject is just Kim.
Who won the prize identifies which student and is integrated into the NP as a modifier. Who lives in Leeds adds information about a sister already identified; it is a supplement, set off by commas.
In looked up the word, up is a one-word PP and the word is the verb's object; the particle can move (looked the word up). In looked up the chimney, up the chimney is one PP and cannot be split.

The words are identical. In the first reading in the tree is inside the object NP, modifying bird; in the second it is an adjunct in the VP. Ambiguity of this kind is ambiguity of constituent structure.
Has is an auxiliary in the perfect, taking a past-participial clause complement; it is a lexical verb of possession taking an NP object in the second.
Outside is a preposition in both: intransitive in the first, transitive with the house as complement in the second, much as a verb may occur with or without an object.
The content clause is an extraposed subject in the first, with dummy it as the subject; in the second it is itself the subject. Meaning is the same; information packaging differs.
Happy is an adjective in both. Attributively it modifies the head child inside the NP; predicatively it is the complement of be. These are the two central functions of adjectives.
